title: Social Media Self-Presentation
hook: A profile photo is body language frozen and multiplied, read by strangers in a fraction of a second and remembered long after you have changed.
why:
For many people, the first time someone sees them is no longer in person. A recruiter looks at a profile on a professional network, a potential date scrolls past a picture on an app, a new colleague looks you up before a meeting, a client checks your photo on a company website. In each case, a single still image is doing the work that a handshake, a voice and a few minutes of conversation used to do.

That image is body language: a face, an expression, a posture, an angle, a setting. But it is body language with unusual properties. It is chosen rather than spontaneous. It is seen by many more people than any real encounter. It is judged in a fraction of a second, without the correction that a conversation would bring. And it lasts, sometimes for years after the person in it has changed. This chapter looks at how quickly faces in photos are judged, how much those judgments matter, how much photos of the same person vary, why other people choose better photos of you than you do, what the feed does to men's sense of their own bodies, how to read other people's curated selves, and how to present yourself honestly. It is the mirror image of the rest of this part: instead of reading others, it is about how you are read when you are not there.

teach.p:
In 2006 Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov showed people photographs of unfamiliar faces for different lengths of time, from a tenth of a second to a full second, and asked them to judge traits such as trustworthiness, competence, likeability, aggressiveness and attractiveness. They compared these quick judgments with judgments made by other people who could look at the same faces for as long as they liked.

The judgments made after a tenth of a second were already closely in line with the untimed ones. Trustworthiness showed the strongest agreement. Giving people more time made little difference to what they concluded. It did make them more confident in their judgments, and slightly more negative.

This does not mean the judgments were accurate. The study measured agreement between viewers, not whether the faces belonged to people who were really trustworthy or competent. Part I's chapter on the face discussed how weak the link between facial appearance and character tends to be. What the study shows is that people form a firm impression of a face almost instantly, and that looking longer mainly increases their confidence in it.

For a profile photo, this has a plain implication. Most people who see it will look for well under a second, scrolling past in a list of other faces. In that moment they will form an impression of whether you seem trustworthy, warm and capable, and they will feel sure of it. The figure here is seen at three quarters, the angle of a typical portrait. A viewer has already decided something about him.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if impressions formed after a tenth of a second differed substantially from those formed without a time limit. Willis and Todorov found they were closely in line, with more time adding confidence rather than changing the judgment.

teach.p:
Snap judgments from faces are not only formed quickly. They can shape real decisions. In 2005 Alexander Todorov and his colleagues showed people pairs of photographs of the winner and runner-up in elections for the United States Senate and House of Representatives, without telling them who the candidates were. Participants were asked which candidate looked more competent, often after seeing the faces for about a second.

The candidate judged more competent from his face had won roughly seven times out of ten Senate races. Judgments of other traits, such as how attractive or likeable a candidate looked, did not predict the results. Only the impression of competence did. The participants knew nothing about the candidates' records or policies. They were responding to faces alone.

Later work has found similar effects in other countries, though with variation. None of this means that voters choose only on faces. It means that the impression a face makes is one influence among many, and that it can be strong enough to matter when other information is weak or the contest is close.

If the faces of experienced politicians can sway elections, the faces in profile photos can certainly sway the smaller decisions made about ordinary people: whom to interview, whom to message, whom to trust with a contract. These impressions are formed from a single image in a single second, and they have little to do with the person's actual competence. The figure here stands upright with hands behind his back, the formal bearing of an official portrait, a pose chosen precisely because of how it is read.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if competence judgments from candidates' faces bore no relation to election outcomes. Todorov and colleagues found they predicted the winner in roughly seven out of ten Senate races, though other factors also mattered.
teach.pullQuote: A face is judged in a fraction of a second, and looking longer mostly makes people more sure of what they already concluded.

teach.p:
It is natural to think of a face as fixed, so that any reasonable photo of you shows more or less the same person. Research on face recognition shows otherwise. In 2011 Rob Jenkins, David White, Xandra van Montfort and Mike Burton collected many everyday photographs of the same individuals, the kind of images found online, and asked people who did not know them to sort the photos by identity.

People who were unfamiliar with the faces greatly overestimated how many different people were in the set, treating photos of the same person as photos of different people. People who knew the individuals sorted them easily. The researchers also found that ratings of attractiveness varied more between different photos of the same person than between different people. Lighting, angle, expression, camera distance and the moment of capture changed faces far more than viewers realised.

Todorov and his colleagues later showed the same thing for impressions of character: different photos of one person can produce quite different judgments of trustworthiness or competence. A face is not one image. It is a range of images, and any single photo samples one point in that range.

This is good news for anyone choosing a profile photo, because it means the photo matters and can be chosen well. It is also a caution for anyone judging others from a photo. The image you are reacting to may be an unlucky moment, a bad angle or an old picture, and the person may look and seem quite different in life. The figure here tilts his head slightly, a small change that alters how a whole face is read.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if different photos of the same person produced consistent impressions. Jenkins and colleagues found that attractiveness varied more across photos of one person than between people, and later work found the same for impressions of character.

teach.p:
If photos vary so much, the obvious step is to choose the best one. The difficulty is that people are not very good at choosing photos of themselves. In 2017 David White, Clare Sutherland and Amy Burton asked people to choose, from a set of their own photographs, the ones they would use for a social media profile, a dating site or a professional network. They also had strangers choose from the same photos. Then other strangers rated the chosen images.

Photos chosen by strangers made better impressions than photos people chose for themselves. The researchers called it the curse of self. When we look at our own photos, we see them through our own feelings about our faces: the feature we dislike, the expression we remember feeling awkward about, the way we think we look. Strangers see what other strangers will see.

This suggests a simple practice. Collect a dozen recent, natural photos of yourself, and ask several people who do not know you well, or who can be frank, to choose the ones that make the best impression for the purpose you have in mind. A professional network, a dating app and a company website may need different choices. Natural expressions tend to work better than posed ones, and a genuine smile, as the chapter on the poker face earlier in this part described, generally helps more than it costs.

It is also worth matching the photo to the setting. A photo taken at a wedding may show you happy and at ease, but cropped onto a professional profile it can look out of place. The figure here stands with weight on one hip, relaxed and at ease, the kind of unguarded posture that a friend's camera often catches and that the person in the picture might never have chosen.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people chose photos of themselves that made better impressions than those chosen by strangers. White, Sutherland and Burton found the reverse.

teach.p:
Social media does not only show others your body. It shows you everyone else's. For men, much of what is shown is a narrow ideal: lean, muscular, often shirtless, photographed in flattering light after a workout, sometimes edited, occasionally enhanced with drugs. Fitness influencers, celebrity transformations and advertising present this body as normal and achievable.

Experiments have found that it affects men who see it. In one 2020 study, Marika Tiggemann and Isabella Anderberg showed young men Instagram images of muscular, bare-chested men, of the same men clothed, or of scenery. Those who saw the bare-chested images were less satisfied with their own bodies afterwards. Other studies have found similar short-term effects, though the size varies and not every study finds them. Surveys link heavy use of appearance-focused social media with concern about muscularity, though they cannot show which comes first.

Part II's chapters dealt with what the body shows when a person is struggling. Here the point is narrower: what you scroll through shapes how you feel about your own body, and therefore how you hold it. A man who has spent half an hour comparing himself with fitness accounts may stand and move differently from one who has not, more self-conscious and less at ease.

The practical steps are simple, if not easy. Notice how you feel after time on particular accounts. Unfollow those that leave you feeling worse. Remember that many such images are the best of hundreds of attempts, taken in ideal conditions. And spend time in places where real bodies are visible, from the gym changing room to the beach, where the range of normal is far wider than any feed suggests. The figure here stands slumped, the posture that can follow a long session of comparison.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's body satisfaction were unaffected by viewing idealised muscular images. Tiggemann and Anderberg found it fell after such images, though effects vary across studies and most measure only the short term.

teach.p:
Every feed is a selection. People post their holidays, promotions, new babies and best photos, and rarely their arguments, rejections, bad days or sleepless nights. Readers know this in principle. In practice, the steady stream of good news shapes their sense of how other people's lives are going.

In 2011 Alexander Jordan, Benoît Monin, Carol Dweck and their colleagues found that people consistently underestimate how often others experience negative emotions, while estimating positive emotions more accurately. Part of the reason was that people tend to hide their negative feelings and show their positive ones, so others see a skewed sample. People who underestimated others' negative experiences more tended to report lower satisfaction with their own lives. The study was not about social media, which magnifies the same skew.

The lesson for reading others is to treat a feed as a highlight reel, not as evidence of how someone is. A friend whose posts are cheerful may be struggling. A colleague whose life looks effortless online may be finding things as hard as you are. You cannot read a person's state from what they choose to post, any more than you could read a man's mood from his best suit.

Changes can be worth noticing, with care. A friend who usually posts often and suddenly goes silent, or whose posts change markedly in tone, may simply be busy or taking a break. It may also be worth a message, in the spirit of the chapters in Part II and Part III on checking in: not a diagnosis, just a question. The figure here slouches low on a sofa, phone in hand, comparing his ordinary evening with everyone else's best moments.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people estimated others' negative emotions as accurately as their positive ones. Jordan and colleagues found people consistently underestimated how often others felt bad, partly because negative feelings are hidden more often.

teach.p:
If impressions from photos are fast, strong and variable, there is a temptation to manage them hard: heavy filters, flattering angles, carefully staged settings, a body that has been edited. Some curation is normal and harmless. Everyone chooses a decent photo rather than an unflattering one. But there are good reasons to keep self-presentation honest.

The first is practical. A photo that does not look like you on a good day creates an expectation that the first meeting cannot meet. On dating apps, this is a familiar source of disappointment. At work, a profile picture that is ten years old makes the first video call slightly awkward. The best photo is one that looks like you as people will meet you.

The second is about the people around you. Your photos often include others, and posting an image of a friend, a colleague or a child shapes how they are seen by people they have never met. Asking before you post, especially for images of children or of people in vulnerable moments, extends to others the care you would want for yourself.

The third is permanence. A post can be found years later by an employer, a partner or a child, and the person you were when you posted it may not be the person you are. It is worth asking, before posting, whether you would be content for this image to represent you in five years. Presence online, like presence in a room, works best when it is congruent: when the image, the words and the person all match. The figure here stands open and at ease, as he might look to anyone who met him in person.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if heavily edited or outdated photos made first meetings go as smoothly as accurate ones. The mismatch between image and person is a common source of disappointment, though this is drawn more from experience than from controlled studies.
teach.pullQuote: The best photo is one that looks like you as people will meet you.

poseGallery.annotation: A tough, posed shot may look confident to you and cold to strangers. A relaxed, natural image usually reads as warmer and just as capable.

poseGallery.doCaption: At ease, weight on one hip
poseGallery.dontCaption: Arms locked for a serious photo
poseGallery.annotation: Strangers choose better photos of you than you do. The unguarded shot a friend took may be the one that works.

poseGallery.doCaption: Phone down, out among real people
poseGallery.dontCaption: Scrolling and comparing on the sofa
poseGallery.annotation: A feed shows everyone's best moments. Time among real bodies and real lives resets the sense of what is normal.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Filming the party through a phone
poseGallery.annotation: A moment spent getting the shot is a moment not spent in it. Take a few photos, then put the phone away.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, looking at the feed together
poseGallery.dontCaption: Lecturing a teenager about his phone
poseGallery.annotation: Teenagers tend to talk more easily side by side than face to face. Curiosity opens a conversation that a lecture closes.

caseStudy:
Callum, thirty-one, was looking for a new job and, after a breakup, had started using a dating app. On both, he used photos he had chosen himself: a serious headshot with his arms folded for the professional network, and for the app a gym selfie taken after months of training, along with a photo from a stag weekend. He had few responses on either.

A friend who worked in recruitment offered to look. She said the headshot made him look severe, and that the gym selfie said more about the gym than about him. She went through his phone and picked out three photos he had never considered: one of him laughing at a barbecue, one of him talking to someone at a friend's wedding, and a plain, smiling photo his sister had taken on a walk.

He was sceptical. He thought he looked tired in one and that his smile was lopsided in another. But he used them. Within a fortnight, two recruiters had contacted him, and conversations on the dating app began to go further. Several people mentioned that he looked friendly.

Around the same time, he noticed that he felt worse about himself on days when he spent time on fitness accounts, and that he had been comparing his body with men who trained for a living. He unfollowed most of them. He kept training, but stopped photographing it. When he met someone from the app for the first time, she said he looked exactly like his pictures, which he decided was the best review a profile could get.
observe: Notice how quickly you form an impression of someone from a profile photo, and how sure of it you feel.
Notice how different you look across several photos taken of you in the same month.
Notice how you feel about your own body after time on particular accounts or feeds.
Notice a friend whose feed looks effortless, and whether you know how they are actually doing.

drills.name: Stranger's Choice
steps: Collect twelve recent, natural photos of yourself, including some you would not choose.
Decide what the photo is for: a professional profile, a dating app or a company page.
Ask three people who do not know you well, or who will be frank, to choose their top two for that purpose.
Compare their choices with your own.
Try one of their choices for a month.
variations: Ask the three people to say, in a word, what each photo makes them think of you, and compare their words with the impression you want to give.
Repeat the exercise for a different purpose, such as a dating profile, and see whether the chosen photos change.
Take some new photos while talking to a friend, rather than posing, and add them to the set before people choose.

drills.name: Feed Audit
steps: Scroll through the accounts you follow for five minutes, noticing how you feel about your body and your life.
List any accounts that reliably leave you feeling worse.
Unfollow or mute at least two of them.
After a week, notice whether anything has changed.
variations: Keep a note for a week of how you feel after each session on social media, in a word, and look for the accounts linked to the worst words.
Follow two accounts that show ordinary bodies, ordinary lives or a hobby you enjoy, and notice whether your feed feels different after a fortnight.
Set a time limit for one app for a week, and notice what you do with the time instead.

drills.name: Behind the Highlights
steps: Choose three friends whose feeds look as if things are going well.
Write down what you actually know about how each is doing, apart from their posts.
Send one of them a message asking how they are, without referring to their posts.
variations: Ask an old friend you have not spoken to in a while how they really are, by phone if you can.
Think of a time when your own feed looked better than your life, and what you would have wanted someone to ask you.
Notice your reaction the next time a friend posts good news, and send them a message about something other than the post.

drills.name: Five-Year Test
steps: Before posting anything about yourself or others this week, pause.
Ask whether you would be content for it to represent you in five years.
If it includes someone else, ask whether they would be content too, or ask them.
Note how often the pause changed what you posted.
variations: Before posting a photo of a group, message each person in it, and notice how many say no or ask for a different one.
Look back at something you posted five years ago and ask whether you would post it now.
Agree a family rule about photos of children, such as no names, schools or locations, and share it with relatives who post.

quiz.q: A friend says he can judge people from profile photos better if he looks at them carefully for a while. What did Willis and Todorov find?
options: Longer viewing made judgments far more accurate, so careful study of a photo pays off
Judgments after a tenth of a second matched untimed ones; more time mainly added confidence
Judgments after a tenth of a second were random and bore no relation to longer ones
Longer viewing made people less confident, because they noticed more contradictory details
quiz.explain: Impressions formed in a tenth of a second were closely in line with untimed ones. More time increased confidence rather than changing the judgment, and the study did not show the judgments were accurate.

quiz.q: In Todorov and colleagues' 2005 study, which judgment from candidates' faces predicted election results?
options: How attractive the candidates looked to the participants
How likeable and friendly the candidates appeared to be
How competent the candidates looked, often after a second
How old the candidates appeared, relative to their rivals
quiz.explain: The candidate judged more competent from his face had won roughly seven of ten Senate races. Judgments of attractiveness and likeability did not predict the results.

quiz.q: What did Jenkins and colleagues find when people sorted everyday photos of unfamiliar faces?
options: They sorted them accurately, because a face looks much the same in every photo
They sorted them accurately when the photos had all been taken by professional photographers
They grouped photos of different people together, because all the faces looked alike
They treated photos of one person as different people, and attractiveness varied widely
quiz.explain: Unfamiliar viewers greatly overestimated the number of people in the set, and attractiveness varied more across photos of one person than between people. Any single photo samples one point in a wide range.

quiz.q: According to White, Sutherland and Burton, who chooses profile photos that make the best impression?
options: Strangers choosing from your photos, rather than you choosing for yourself
You, because you know which photos look most like you in your everyday life
Close family, because they know you best and see you most kindly
A professional photographer, choosing from a studio session alone
quiz.explain: Photos chosen by strangers made better impressions than those people chose for themselves. The researchers called it the curse of self: we see our own photos through our feelings about our faces.

quiz.q: A friend's posts show a promotion, a holiday and a new flat, and you feel your own life is falling behind. What does Jordan and colleagues' research suggest?
options: Your friend's life is probably going as well as the posts suggest, so your feeling is accurate
People underestimate how often others feel bad, partly because negative feelings are hidden
People overestimate others' negative feelings, so your friend is probably even happier
Comparing yourself with others is harmless, because people know that posts are selective
quiz.explain: People consistently underestimate others' negative experiences, partly because those are hidden more than positive ones. A feed magnifies that skew, so it is poor evidence of how someone is really doing.

quiz.q: You need a new photo for a professional profile. Which approach fits this chapter best?
options: Ask a few frank people to choose from several recent, natural photos for that purpose
Use the photo you like best of yourself, since you know your own face better than others
Use a heavily edited photo, since first impressions from photos are formed so very fast
Use an old photo from your best year, since impressions do not change much over time
quiz.explain: Others choose better photos of us than we do, and photos vary widely. A recent, natural photo also matches how people will meet you, which avoids a mismatch later.

quiz.q: In Tiggemann and Anderberg's 2020 study, what happened to young men who saw Instagram images of muscular, bare-chested men?
options: They became much more satisfied with their own bodies and more motivated to exercise
They were less satisfied with their own bodies than men who saw other images
They showed no change at all compared with men who saw the same men fully clothed
They became more critical of the men in the images, but not of their own bodies
quiz.explain: Young men who saw the bare-chested images were less satisfied with their own bodies afterwards. Other studies have found similar short-term effects, though the size varies.

quiz.q: A landlord asks applicants for a photo and rejects one because his selfie, taken at night in a car, looks shifty. What fits this chapter best?
options: Trust the impression, since people can judge trustworthiness reliably in a tenth of a second
Stop judging from photos, and use the same references and questions for every applicant
Ask the applicant for a better photo, and decide on the basis of the second one instead
Choose applicants who send professional photos, since they show who takes things seriously
quiz.explain: Photos of the same person vary more than photos of different people, and snap impressions agree between viewers without being accurate. References and consistent questions say far more about a tenant than a selfie.

quiz.q: Someone says that Todorov's election study shows that candidates who look competent really are more competent. What did the study actually measure?
options: Whether impressions of competence from faces predicted who won, not whether the winners were competent
Whether the winning candidates went on to perform better in office than the candidates who lost
Whether voters who knew the candidates' records rated their faces as looking more competent
Whether competent-looking candidates had higher scores on tests of intelligence and knowledge
quiz.explain: Participants judged competence from faces alone, and those judgments predicted election results. The study shows the power of the impression, not that the impression was correct.

reflection.prompt: Look at one specific profile photo you currently use, on any platform. Describe it as a stranger would: your expression, posture, angle, clothing and setting. What impression do you think it gives in the first second? Who chose it, and why? Then think about the accounts you follow, and describe how you usually feel about your own body and life after scrolling through them. What one change would you make to how you present yourself or what you look at?
reflection.guidance: Most people find it hard to see their own photos as strangers do, which is exactly the point of the curse of self. Be specific about what is in the image rather than how you feel about it. If you can, ask someone else to describe it too, and compare their description with yours.

failureMode: The first failure is to believe that people will look at your photo carefully, when most will judge it in a fraction of a second and feel sure of their judgment. The second is to choose your own photos and trust your own preferences, when strangers reliably choose better. The third is to judge others confidently from a single image, when photos of the same person vary more than photos of different people. The fourth is to let a feed of idealised male bodies set your sense of what is normal, and to carry that comparison into how you hold yourself. The fifth is to read others' curated highlights as evidence of their real lives. And the sixth is to present an image so edited or out of date that the person who arrives cannot match it.

moreCases.title: The photo from fifteen years ago
moreCases.scene:
Stuart, fifty-five, is a management consultant who works mostly on his own, winning clients through his professional profile and
  recommendations. His profile photo was taken by a professional photographer fifteen years ago, when he had more hair, less grey and a sharper jaw.
  He likes it. It looks, he thinks, like the version of himself that clients should hire.

  He has noticed something odd about his first video calls with new clients. In the first few seconds, after the camera connects, there is often a
  small pause, a flicker of something on the other person's face, and then a slightly too bright "Hello, Stuart!". Once or twice someone has said,
  "Oh, hello, I wasn't sure I had the right call." He has started to dread that moment. He reads the flicker as disappointment, and he has begun to
  wonder whether clients find him less impressive in person than his reputation suggests.

  A former client who has become a friend, Anjali, mentions the photo over lunch. She tells him, laughing, that when they first met on video she had
  thought for a moment that his son had joined the call by mistake.

  Stuart is stung, and then thoughtful. He realises that every new client has met two people: the man in the photo, and then him.

He has also kept the photo on his company's website, his conference badges and the back of his book, so that by now there are hundreds of copies of a man who no longer exists.

He also notices that he has started switching his camera on a few seconds late, after the other person has appeared, as if to delay the moment of comparison.
moreCases.misread:
Stuart read the flicker on new clients' faces as disappointment in him, and began to doubt how he came across. They were reacting to the gap between a fifteen-year-old photo and the man in front of them.

He also read his own discomfort at the start of calls as nerves about meeting new people, when it was the strain of being compared, every time, with a younger man.

The clients, for their part, read the mismatch as a small oddity and moved on, but the first minute of every call was spent adjusting rather than listening. Stuart read that minute as the verdict.
moreCases.betterRead:
Willis and Todorov found that impressions from faces form in a fraction of a second and are held with growing confidence. Every client had formed an impression of Stuart from the old photo, and the first second of every call broke it. The flicker was surprise, not judgment, but it put both of them slightly on the back foot. The better approach was the one the chapter recommends: a photo that looks like you as people will meet you. Following White, Sutherland and Burton's finding, Stuart gathered a dozen recent, natural photos and asked three people who did not know him well to choose. They picked one taken by his daughter at a garden party, grey hair and all, in which he was listening to someone and smiling. The flicker disappeared from his first calls. Two new clients mentioned that he looked approachable.

He also updated the photo on his website and his conference badge, so that every new contact met the same man.

moreCases.title: The tenant in the selfie
moreCases.scene:
Hilary, sixty-one, owns three flats that she lets herself. When a flat comes up, she advertises it online and asks applicants to send a short
  message and a photo of themselves, so that she can, as she puts it, get a feel for who she is dealing with. For the flat above the bakery, she gets
  twenty applications in two days.

  One applicant, Kai, twenty-six, a hospital porter, sends a long, polite message and a selfie taken at night in a car, lit from below by the phone
  screen, unsmiling. Hilary thinks he looks shifty and does not reply. Another applicant, a man in his thirties, sends a bright, smiling photo in a
  suit, taken at a wedding. He seems, she thinks, like a nice, reliable young man. She lets him the flat.

  Within four months he is two months behind on rent and has sublet the second bedroom without telling her. When she finally gets him out, the flat
  needs redecorating.

  When she re-advertises, Kai applies again. His references, which she asks for this time, are excellent: three years in his last flat, a landlord
  who calls him the best tenant he has had. She meets him for a viewing. He is warm, a little shy and very careful about the condition of the flat.

She had also, without thinking about it, rejected two other applicants whose photos were taken in poor light, and accepted one for her previous flat who had looked, she said at the time, "like a lovely girl", and who had been.

Hilary's daughter, when she hears about it, points out that the wedding photo had probably been taken by a professional, and the car selfie by a man on his break at the end of a night shift.
moreCases.misread:
Hilary read Kai's dark, unsmiling selfie as a sign of an untrustworthy character, and the smiling wedding photo of the other applicant as evidence of reliability. Both readings came from single images, and both were wrong.

She also read her own confidence in her judgment as experience, when it was the ordinary confidence that snap judgments bring with them.

She also read the second applicant's suit and smile as a promise about his behaviour, when they were a record of one good afternoon at a wedding. Neither photo told her anything about paying rent.
moreCases.betterRead:
Jenkins and colleagues found that different photos of the same person vary more in how they are judged than photos of different people, and Todorov's later work showed the same for impressions of character. A selfie lit from below in a car at night would make almost anyone look shifty; a professional photo at a wedding would flatter almost anyone. Willis and Todorov's work showed how quickly such impressions form and how confident they feel, but their studies measured agreement between viewers, not accuracy. Hilary's better approach was to stop asking for photos at all. She now asks applicants for references and proof of income, uses the same questions for everyone, and meets shortlisted applicants for a viewing. She let the flat to Kai. He has been there two years.

She also told the other landlords in her street about the change, and two of them stopped asking for photos too.

moreCases.title: The son and the feed
moreCases.scene:
Tom, forty-seven, has noticed changes in his son, Luke, sixteen, over the past six months. Luke has started going to the gym five or six times a
  week, which Tom was pleased about at first. Then he noticed that Luke had begun refusing family meals with pasta or bread, weighing his food, and
  spending long stretches in his room looking at his phone. One evening, passing Luke's door, Tom sees him standing in front of the mirror with his
  shirt off, turning from side to side, frowning.

  When Tom glances at Luke's phone, left on the kitchen table, the screen is full of fitness accounts: young men with very low body fat and very large
  muscles, many of them shirtless, many of them selling supplements or training plans. Luke has saved dozens of posts.

  Tom's first instinct is to make a joke about it, as his own father would have done. His second is to confiscate the phone. He does neither. He
  tells his partner, Nadia, what he has seen, and they agree they need to talk to Luke, but neither of them is sure how.

  That weekend, on a drive to his grandmother's, Luke says, out of nowhere, that he hates how he looks, and that everyone at the gym is bigger than
  him.

Tom has also noticed that Luke has stopped wanting to go swimming with his younger brother, which he used to love, and wears a hoodie even on warm days.

Nadia remembers that Luke had once said, a few months earlier, that he could never look like the men at the gym "without help", and that she had not asked what he meant.
moreCases.misread:
Tom's first reading was that Luke's new habits were a healthy enthusiasm that had gone a little far. His instincts, to joke or to confiscate, would have treated it as a phase to be mocked or a rule to be enforced, rather than as distress.

Luke, for his part, read the men on his phone as normal and himself as failing, without knowing how those images had been made.

Nadia's first reading, when Tom told her, was that Luke was simply being a teenager, which was partly true and would have missed the part that mattered.
moreCases.betterRead:
Tiggemann and Anderberg found that young men who viewed Instagram images of muscular, bare-chested men were less satisfied with their own bodies afterwards, and other studies have found similar effects, though their size varies. A feed of men who train and diet for a living, some of them edited or using drugs, can quietly become the standard a teenager measures himself against. Tom's better response, in the car, was to listen rather than reassure, and to ask what Luke was seeing online. Later, sitting side by side with him, he looked through the feed with Luke and talked about how the photos were made. They agreed to unfollow some accounts together. Because Luke's eating had changed and his distress seemed real, Tom and Nadia also took him to see their GP, who referred him for support. Tom did not try to work out what was wrong himself.

Luke still goes to the gym, three times a week now, and eats with the family. The fitness accounts on his phone have mostly been replaced by football clips.

moreCases.title: The friend whose feed was perfect
moreCases.scene:
Oliver, thirty-five, has known Rob since university. They used to see each other every few weeks, but since Rob moved two hundred miles away
  for a new job, they have kept in touch mostly through social media. Over the past year, Rob's feed has been a run of good news: a promotion, a new
  house, a baby daughter, a holiday in Portugal with the baby asleep on his chest by a pool.

  Oliver, whose own year has included a redundancy and a breakup, finds the feed hard to look at. Each post makes him feel further behind. He stops
  liking the posts and stops messaging, partly out of envy and partly because he cannot think what to say that would not sound like complaining. He
  assumes Rob is too busy and too happy to notice.

  In November, a mutual friend mentions that Rob has been having a very hard time. His partner has been seriously unwell since the birth, Rob has been
  caring for her and the baby while holding down the new job, and he has barely slept in months. He has been seeing his GP for support. The holiday
  photo was from the one good week of the year.

  Oliver sits with that for a long time. He realises he has not asked Rob how he is in eight months.

He has also, he realises, been posting less himself, and only the good things: a run, a meal out, a view from a walk. Anyone looking at his own feed would have no idea about the redundancy.

Rob had posted the holiday photo, the friend says, because his partner had asked him to, so that their families would see that they were all right.
moreCases.misread:
Oliver read Rob's feed as evidence that Rob's life was going brilliantly, and read his own silence as a reasonable response to someone too busy and happy to miss him. Rob, unseen, may well have read Oliver's silence as a friendship fading.

And he read his own envy as a reason to step back, when it was a sign of how much the friendship still mattered to him.

Rob had also read Oliver's silence, he said later, as Oliver being busy with a life of his own. Each man had been reading the other's feed, and neither had seen the other.
moreCases.betterRead:
Jordan and colleagues found that people consistently underestimate how often others experience negative emotions, partly because people tend to show their positive feelings and hide their negative ones, and that those who underestimated others' struggles more tended to be less satisfied with their own lives. A feed concentrates that skew into a highlight reel. Oliver compared his worst year with Rob's best week. The better reading treats a feed as a selection, not a report, and treats silence from an old friend as something to break, not to wait out. Oliver sent Rob a message that evening: "I've been a rubbish friend this year. How are you, really?" Rob rang him back the next day, and they talked for an hour. Oliver visited at Christmas, and helped with the washing up while Rob slept.

Oliver also started telling a few close friends the truth about his own year, and found that two of them had been having hard years too, behind feeds that looked fine.

workedReading.title: Posting photos from a family party
workedReading.scene:
Rosa, forty-four, has organised her father's eightieth birthday party in the back room of a local pub, with forty guests, three generations and a cake shaped like his old allotment shed. She has taken more than two hundred photos on her phone, and her family has asked her to post some so that relatives abroad can see. Sitting on the train home, she starts to choose. The photos include her father, who loves being photographed; her brother, Michael, who has just come out of hospital and is thin and pale; her niece, Bea, fifteen, who hates photos of herself; her cousin's toddler; and a dozen friends of her father's whom she barely knows. Rosa wants to share the joy of the day. She also knows that everyone in the photos will be seen by people they have never met, for a long time, and she decides to take the choosing as seriously as the party.

She has posted family photos before without asking anyone, and once had to take one down after a cousin rang in tears because her former partner had seen it. She does not want that again.

She also remembers how she felt when a friend posted a photo of her at a wedding, mid-mouthful, without asking, and how long it took for the comments to stop.

steps.label: Look at what you have
steps.text:
She scrolls through the photos and notices how much they vary. In some, her father looks frail; in others, telling a story with his hands, he looks twenty years younger. Jenkins and colleagues found that photos of the same person vary more than people expect, and she can see it in every face on her phone. She picks a shortlist of twenty in which people look the way they did at the party: happy, at ease and themselves.

She also notices that the photos she likes best of herself are not the ones her sister likes best of her, and remembers the research on choosing your own photos.

steps.label: Ask whose photo it is
steps.text:
Before posting anything with someone else in it, she messages them. Her father says yes to everything. Michael asks her not to post any close-ups of him, because he does not want people asking about his health; he is happy with a group photo where he is at the back, laughing. Bea replies with a single word, "no", and then, a minute later, "the one where I'm behind Grandad is fine".

She does not ask Bea why. A teenager's no is a complete answer, and Bea has given her an alternative that works.

She also tells Michael which group photo she has in mind and sends it to him first, so that he can see exactly how he looks before anyone else does.

steps.label: Check the children
steps.text:
The toddler appears in several photos. Rosa messages her cousin, who is happy for one photo to go up but asks that it not show the name of the nursery on the child's jumper. Rosa crops it. She also checks that none of the photos shows the pub's name and the date together with the child, since she does not know everyone who will see the post.

She also thinks about her father's friends, some of whom are not on social media at all and may not expect to appear there. She leaves out the photos of the ones she could not reach.

She also checks her privacy settings, which have not been changed in years, and restricts the post to friends and family.

steps.label: Apply the five-year test
steps.text:
She imagines each photo being seen in five years' time, by a future employer, a new partner or the person themselves. One photo of her father's old friend, mid-sentence with a pint and his eyes half closed, is funny now and unkind later. She leaves it out. One photo of the whole family around the cake, everyone laughing, will be lovely in five years and in fifty. That one goes first.

She also applies the test to herself. One photo of her, flushed and mid-laugh, is unflattering and entirely true to the day. She keeps it.

She also thinks of Bea in five years, at nineteen, and is glad that no photo of her at fifteen will be waiting for her.

steps.label: Choose what to leave out
steps.text:
She ends with eight photos, from two hundred. The ones she leaves out include several in which people look less than their best, the one Bea vetoed, the close-ups of Michael and every photo that she would not want posted of herself. She notices that this is much the same rule White, Sutherland and Burton's work implies: other people are better judges of how they want to be seen than you are.

She also sends the full set of two hundred privately to her father, who wants to see every one.

steps.label: Write the caption
steps.text:
She writes a short caption naming the occasion and thanking everyone who came, and tags only those who have agreed to be tagged. She avoids anything that would invite questions about Michael. She turns off comments on the photo of the toddler and leaves them on for the others, so that relatives abroad can send their wishes.

She also avoids the usual phrases about the best day ever, because Michael's illness made the day harder for some of the family than the photos show.

She also adds a line inviting family members to message her for the full album, so that anyone who wants every photo can have them without all of them being public.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Within an hour, her aunt in Canada has commented, and her father's oldest friend has sent a message saying he is going to print the cake photo. Michael tells her later that he was grateful she asked. Bea, without comment, likes the photo in which she is behind her grandfather. Rosa reflects that the eight photos tell the story of the day better than two hundred would have, and that nobody in them will wish they were not there.

She also notices that she enjoyed the choosing, and that it made her look at the day again more carefully than she would have otherwise.

Her father asks her to print the eight photos, which he puts on the mantelpiece in the order she posted them.

moreFailures.title: Treating likes as a verdict
moreFailures.body:
Many people watch the reaction to their posts closely: how many likes, how fast, from whom, and who stayed silent. A post that gets fewer likes than usual can feel like a social judgment, and a friend who does not react can feel like a friend who has cooled. But reactions on social media depend on far more than the post or the person: on the time of day it was posted, on what the platform chose to show to whom, on how busy people were, on whether they saw it at all. Much of what you see as silence is people who never saw your post. Like any nonverbal cue, reactions are ambiguous and easily over-read, and treating them as a measure of how much you are liked is one of the quickest ways to make a feed feel worse. If you want to know how a friendship is going, ask the friend.

If you find yourself refreshing a post to check its reactions, close the app for an hour. The number will not mean more when you come back.

Many platforms now let you hide like counts, which some people find makes posting feel lighter.

moreFailures.title: Posting other people without asking
moreFailures.body:
It is easy to post a photo of a friend, a colleague or a family member without a second thought, especially when you look good in it. But each photo shapes how that person is seen by people they may never meet: future employers, new partners, people who wish them harm. The person in the photo may be recovering from an illness, may have reasons to keep their location private, may simply dislike how they look, or may not want people to know they were there. Children cannot consent at all, and images of them, their schools and their routines can travel far. Before posting anyone else, ask, as Rosa did. Accept a no without argument. And if you are tagged in something you would rather not be, it is fine to ask for it to come down.

A simple rule: post others as you would want to be posted, and when in doubt, leave it out.

moreFailures.title: Checking the candidate's photo before the interview
moreFailures.body:
Many recruiters and managers look up candidates online before an interview, and the profile photo is the first thing they see. Todorov and colleagues found that impressions of competence from faces alone predicted election results, and Willis and Todorov found that such impressions form in a fraction of a second and grow in confidence with more looking, not in accuracy. A recruiter who glances at a photo has formed an impression before reading a word of the application, and the chapter on interviews earlier in this part described how first impressions shape the interviewer's manner and the candidate's performance. If you make decisions about people, consider not looking at photos until after you have assessed what they have done and said, and keep any online checks to what is relevant to the job.

If you do look, look at everyone in the same way and at the same stage, so that no candidate is judged on a photo the others did not have to pass.

moreFailures.title: Photographing instead of being there
moreFailures.body:
At a concert, a party, a child's school play or a beautiful view, many people spend much of the moment looking at it through a phone, getting the shot. Part of the motive is the feed: the moment becomes something to present. The cost falls on the moment itself, and on the people in it. A father filming the nativity play is a father whose child, looking out from the stage, sees a phone rather than a face. A friend photographing the meal is a friend not talking. None of this means never taking photos. It means noticing when the camera has taken over from attention, taking a few pictures and putting the phone away, and letting some moments go unrecorded. The best photos of most occasions are often taken by someone else, of you being there.

A good test is to ask yourself, afterwards, whether you remember the moment or the photo.

Some families agree that one person will take the photos at an event, so that everyone else can simply be there.

questions.q: What makes a good profile photo?
questions.a:
One that looks like you as people will meet you, on a good day. That usually means a recent photo, head and shoulders, in good, soft light, with a natural expression, such as the face you make when you are listening to someone you like or laughing at something real. Avoid photos that are many years old, heavily filtered, cropped from a group or taken from an unflattering low angle. The most useful step, from White, Sutherland and Burton's work, is to let other people choose: collect a dozen recent, natural photos and ask several people who do not know you well, or who will be frank, to pick the best for the purpose. Their choices will usually make a better impression than yours, because they see what strangers will see.

And update it every few years, or whenever you change enough that someone meeting you might be surprised.

If you use the same photo across several sites, people who meet you will have one consistent impression to match, which helps.

questions.q: Should I smile in a professional profile photo?
questions.a:
Usually, yes, but moderately. A warm, genuine smile tends to make people seem approachable and trustworthy, and a hard, unsmiling face with the chin raised, the classic serious headshot, can read as cold or arrogant. The chapter on the poker face earlier in this part described Wang and colleagues' finding that broad smiles made people seem warmer but less competent than slight ones, especially when the stakes were high. For a professional profile, a slight, natural smile is a good default. The best way to get one is not to force it but to be photographed while talking to someone or thinking about something pleasant. Then let other people choose the photo in which the smile looks most like yours.

If you are photographed for work, ask the photographer to chat to you while they shoot, which tends to bring out a more natural face.

For a dating profile, the same principle holds: a real smile in a real moment beats any posed expression.

questions.q: Is it wrong to edit my photos?
questions.a:
Light editing, such as adjusting brightness, cropping or correcting colour, is ordinary and harmless. The trouble starts when editing changes the face or body itself: slimming, smoothing, enlarging, reshaping. Edited images set an expectation that the first meeting cannot meet, and on dating apps and at work that mismatch is a familiar source of disappointment. They can also feed the comparisons this chapter describes, for you and for people who see them, because a heavily edited body presented as natural becomes part of someone else's idea of normal. A useful test is whether someone who met you the day after seeing the photo would recognise you immediately and feel that it was a fair likeness.

If you are unsure, ask a friend whether the edited photo looks like you. If they hesitate, use the unedited one.

And if you post for work, remember that clients will compare the photo with the person on their first video call, as Stuart's did.

questions.q: How can I tell whether social media is affecting how I feel about my body?
questions.a:
Notice how you feel before and after time on particular accounts, as the feed audit in this chapter suggests. If you regularly feel worse about your body after scrolling, if you find yourself comparing your shape with people who are paid to look a certain way, or if you are changing what you eat or how you train because of what you see, the feed is probably playing a part. Unfollowing or muting accounts that reliably make you feel worse is a simple first step. If the worry about your body is taking up a lot of your thoughts, affecting your eating, your mood or your relationships, or leading you to consider supplements or drugs, talk to someone you trust and see your doctor. You do not need to work out what is wrong first.

It can also help to spend time with people whose bodies vary, in person, which is a useful corrective to a feed that shows only one kind.

If a friend tells you they are struggling with how they look, listen without comparing or reassuring too quickly, and ask what would help.

questions.q: Should employers look at candidates' social media?
questions.a:
If they do, they should do it carefully, consistently and for reasons connected to the job. A profile photo invites exactly the snap judgments described in this chapter, and impressions formed from a face before reading an application can shape the whole process. Many organisations prefer not to look at photos at all until after a decision, or to have someone other than the decision-maker carry out any checks and report only what is relevant, such as public conduct that would affect the role. Rules on this vary between countries, and it is worth checking them. If you are a candidate, it is sensible to assume that your public profiles may be seen, and to keep them as you would be happy for a future employer to see them.

And if you are the candidate, a current, natural photo is still the safest choice, since it matches the person who will arrive.

Whoever looks, it is worth writing down what was checked and why, so that the process can be explained if anyone asks.

questions.q: How can I talk to a teenager about what they see online?
questions.a:
With curiosity rather than a lecture, and preferably side by side rather than face to face. Teenagers often find it easier to talk in the car, on a walk or while doing something together, as Luke did. Ask what they are watching and what they like about it, and listen to the answer before offering a view. Look at the feed with them, if they are willing, and talk about how the images are made: lighting, angles, editing, the training and diet behind them, and the products being sold. Share your own experience of comparing yourself with others. Avoid mocking or banning, which tend to drive things underground. If you notice changes in eating, mood or behaviour that worry you, talk to your GP, who can help you decide what support is needed.

It also helps to be honest about your own habits. Teenagers notice quickly when the adult lecturing them about phones is looking at one.

And remember that you do not need to be an expert on social media to help. Your attention and your calm matter more than your knowledge of the apps.

watch.title: Black Mirror: Nosedive Featurette
watch.notice: A world in which every interaction is rated. Notice the fixed smiles and performed warmth, and how self-presentation becomes exhausting when it never stops.

reviewPrompt: This week, ask three frank people to choose your profile photo, and unfollow two accounts that leave you feeling worse.
